Brief for the Director

1 · What customers say

Complaints are about waiting: delays, cancellations, lost bags, and above all customer service ("on hold for hours"). Praise goes to staff who fixed a problem.

2 · Can software replace reading?

Not yet. It misses half of the complaints. Use it to sort and prioritise, and keep people for the unclear tweets.

3 · How airlines compare

US Airways is worst (78 % negative). American / US Airways have a service problem, and United / JetBlue have an operations problem.
Act first
  1. Fix the phone bottleneck on disruption days (call-backs, self-rebooking).
  2. Auto-score negative tweets and answer stranded passengers within minutes.
  3. Share daily delay / missed-connection complaints with United and JetBlue operations.
  4. Fix the data: the airline label, the damaged text, and repeat complainers.

Part A · Cleaning the tweets

A1

What breaks a tokenizer

FeatureTweetsTreatment
@handles100 %removed
#hashtags16 %keep word, drop #
links8 %removed
contractions (can't)13 %→ "can not"
&amp; entities5 %unescaped
emojis3 %→ words (emo_enraged_face)
sooooo0.7 %→ "soo"
A naive split() keeps handles as words, splits links into junk and turns can't into can + t. Also found: the file replaced cancel / late / booking with category names ("Cancelled Flightled"), so I undid that.
A2

Stop words vs negation

TweetNegations removedNegations kept
flight was not good"flight good" → +0.44−0.34
not bad for a red-eye"bad red eye" → −0.54+0.43
Removing not / no flips the meaning. On the 33 % of tweets with a negation, agreement with humans drops 53.5 % → 41.1 %. My final list keeps negations, but, very and too.
A3

Stemming vs lemmatization

WordStemLemma
unitedunit ✗unite ✗ → protected
serviceservicservice
flyingflifly
customers / customscustom (merged ✗)kept apart
Vocabulary 10,992 →8,3248,867
Stemming shrinks the vocabulary more, but gives non-words and merges different words. Lemmatization chosen, with airline names protected.
A4

Cost of each cleaning step

The full NLTK stop list goes too far: tweets drop from 16 to 8.6 words and 25 become empty. My list keeps 9.1 words, and only 16 tweets end up empty (they had no content anyway).

Part B · What customers say

B5

Raw vs cleaned top words

Raw counts are dominated by to, the and airline @handles. 100 % of tweets @-mention an airline, so the data was collected by searching airline handles, not general talk about flying.
B6

What separates negative from positive

Flight, service, customer and help are frequent in both classes. Raw frequency can't separate them, and the negative class is 4× bigger.
B6

Distinctive words (TF-IDF)

Negative = waiting and disruption (hour, hold, delay, cancel, bag). Positive = gratitude (thank, great, love).
B7

Phrases in negative tweets

hold hour (phone queue), miss connection (hubs), gate agent, check bag: each points to a specific problem a single word can't show. A flipped pair: "no worries" is made of two negative words, but 70 % of tweets with it are positive.
B8

Word cloud vs bar chart

Show the Director the bar chart. It gives exact order and counts. The cloud makes long words look important ("not" is really 4× "customer").

Part C · Can a sentiment tool read them?

C9

VADER vs human labels

54 % agreement, which is worse than always saying "negative" (63 %). It misses half the complaints, and neutral is the hardest class. The single overall figure hides this.
C10

Why VADER disagrees

tweets %
cause
airline words not in lexicon 884 32.3
other 763 27.8
negation 591 21.6
polite / request words (help, please, thanks) 345 12.6
mixed feelings 109 4.0
sarcasm 48 1.8
Biggest cause: airline words (delayed, cancelled, hold) that score 0. Fix: an airline lexicon raises agreement from 54 % → 59 % and catches 59 % of complaints.
C11

Three tweets that fool VADER

My tweetTruthVADER
"Great, another 4 hour delay. Thanks so much!"negpositive
"I wouldn't say the crew was unhelpful…"posneutral
"3 hours on the tarmac, missed my connection… Best trip ever!"negpositive
Sarcasm, double negation and airline-specific words: the meaning is in context, not in the words.
C12

Can we trust the labels?

26 % of labels have low rater confidence. On confident labels, agreement rises to 59 %; on uncertain ones it is only 43 %. Part of the "error" is label noise.

Part D · Comparing the airlines

D13

Customer service vs operations

The idea holds: American & US Airways = customer service problem; JetBlue & United = operations (late/cancelled).
D14

Count vs share

United has the most complaints, but US Airways has the worst share (78 % negative). Report the share, with the count beside it.
D15

Over time

Spike on 22–23 Feb (74 % negative), partly because American's tweets only start on 22 Feb. The data shows what (cancellations, then service), not why.
D16

Who to answer first

Score = reason (cancelled/lost bag 3) + urgent words like stuck, gate, now (2) + flight no. (1) + retweets (≤3). That gives 823 tweets to answer now.

Part E · Limits of this data

E17

How the data could mislead

  • Only people who choose to tweet, and complainers tweet more
  • American covered for 3 days only; uneven volumes
  • Mislabelled airline, damaged text, 26 % uncertain labels
Trust least: American's customer-service result.
E18

Data from today

  • Twitter → X; complaints moved to apps & chat
  • US Airways and Virgin America no longer exist
  • New topics: refunds, fees, app rebooking
The pattern (delays, bags, service) would likely stay the same.
E19

Replace the manual team?

No. Use the tool to triage.
  • It misses half the complaints
  • But it's 90 % right when it says "negative" and instant
  • Humans check the uncertain tweets

Part F · Extra insights

F1

"Delta" is really JetBlue

99.7 % of "Delta" tweets are sent to @JetBlue. Action: fix the label and check labels against the @handle.
F2

11 % of text is damaged

1,552 tweets have "cancel / late / booking" replaced by category names. Action: recover the original text, or the models will learn the label from the text.
F3

The phone line drives anger

Phone/hold tweets are 93 % negative (vs 63 %). The worst are US Airways at 14 % and American at 11 %. Action: call-backs and self-rebooking on disruption days.
F4

"Can't Tell" = 13 % of complaints

These are general "never again" tweets (19.5 % at JetBlue) that nobody owns. Action: send them to a retention team.
F5

A few users shape the numbers

77 accounts wrote 7.8 % of tweets, some 100 % negative; the top account is a news bot. Action: track per customer and remove bots.
